claimSlots.statement: The shoulder complex comprises the humerus, scapula and clavicle, articulating at the glenohumeral, acromioclavicular and sternoclavicular joints; the sternoclavicular joint is the only bony articulation between the upper limb and the axial skeleton.

lesson.title: Shoulder anatomy a trainer needs
lesson.summary: A working map of the shoulder: three bones, four joints, the cuff that keeps the ball centred, and the big muscles that move the arm.
objectives: Name the bones and joints of the shoulder in plain words and in standard terms.
Explain why the ball-and-socket joint trades stability for range.
Describe what the rotator cuff does as a group.
Find the main landmarks on yourself and, with permission, on a client.

blocks.content: This lesson gives you a working map of the shoulder: where the bones meet, what keeps the ball in its socket, and which muscles do the moving. Every later lesson in this module uses this map.
Three bones, four places they meet

Three bones make the shoulder: the upper arm bone (humerus), the shoulder blade (scapula) and the collarbone (clavicle). They meet at three joints. The ball-and-socket joint (glenohumeral joint) joins the arm to the shoulder blade. The acromioclavicular joint joins the collarbone to the top of the shoulder blade. The sternoclavicular joint joins the collarbone to the breastbone, and it is the only bony link between the arm and the rest of the skeleton.

The shoulder blade also slides over the back of the ribcage. Coaches often call this the scapulothoracic joint, but it is not a joint in the usual sense: there is no joint capsule, only muscle and soft tissue between the shoulder blade and the ribs.

content.caption: The three bones and the four places they meet, seen from the front and from behind.

blocks.content: The socket on the shoulder blade (the glenoid) is shallow and small compared with the ball at the top of the humerus. A rim of fibrous cartilage, the labrum, deepens the socket, and a joint capsule with its ligaments surrounds the joint.

A picture that works for clients: the ball sits on a saucer, not in a cup. The saucer lets the arm move a long way in almost every direction. The cost is that something has to keep the ball on the saucer.
Four muscles form the rotator cuff: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis. Each one starts on the shoulder blade and attaches close to the joint at the top of the humerus.
Working together, the cuff muscles press the ball into the socket and help keep it centred while larger muscles move the arm. Researchers call this pressing effect concavity compression.

content.label: Coach note
content.text: Think of the cuff as a team. You will hear people blame one cuff muscle for every shoulder complaint. This lesson keeps it simple: the cuff's shared job is to keep the ball centred.

blocks.content: Larger muscles produce most of the arm's force. The deltoid raises the arm. The pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi pull the arm toward and across the body. The trapezius and serratus anterior move and steady the shoulder blade, so the socket follows the ball.

content.caption: The rotator cuff close to the joint, and the larger muscles that move the arm and the shoulder blade.

blocks.content: Big range plus a shallow socket means control matters as much as mobility. On the gym floor your job is to load the range a client can control, and to build both the muscles that move the arm and the muscles that steady it.
Find the landmarks on yourself first. With a client, ask before you touch, say what you are touching, and offer to let them find it themselves.

content: Follow the collarbone out from the base of the neck to the bony point at the top of the shoulder (acromion).
Find the ridge that runs across the back of the shoulder blade (spine of the scapula).
Find the bottom tip of the shoulder blade (inferior angle). Keep a finger near it while the arm rises, and feel it move.
Find the front of the shoulder below the collarbone, where the ball sits in front of the socket.

blocks.content: Use plain names with clients and standard names with clinicians. "The ball-and-socket joint" and "the glenohumeral joint" are the same thing. Saying both helps when a client brings you notes from a physiotherapist or doctor.

content.label: Stop and refer
content.text: This lesson tells you where things are and what they do. It does not tell you what is wrong. If a client points to a painful spot, describe where it is and how it behaves; never name an injury. Stop shoulder work for the session and refer when a warning sign appears. After a fall or impact, an arm the client cannot move or a shoulder that looks out of place: emergency services now. Other new pain after an injury, pins and needles that do not go away, or a new inability to lift the arm themselves: an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 today. See "When to refer out".

content.prompt: Which joint joins the upper arm bone to the shoulder blade?
content.explanation: The glenohumeral joint is the ball-and-socket joint between the humerus and the glenoid of the shoulder blade.

content.prompt: What deepens the shallow socket of the shoulder?
content.explanation: The labrum is a rim of fibrous cartilage around the glenoid that makes the socket deeper.

content.prompt: As a group, what does the rotator cuff do while the arm moves?
options: It produces most of the force for heavy overhead lifts
It presses the ball into the socket and helps keep it centred
It locks the shoulder blade so it cannot move
content.explanation: The cuff's shared job is to compress the ball into the socket and keep it centred while larger muscles move the arm.

content.label: Talk it through
content.text: A client points to the front of the shoulder and asks: "Is that my rotator cuff?" What do you say? A good answer describes the area in plain words, says that you do not diagnose, and asks how it behaves in training. If it hurts, or if any warning sign is present, stop and refer.
